newsitem.title: GHANA: One killed, office burnt in Ghana campaign unrest.
newsitem.headline: One killed, office burnt in Ghana campaign unrest.

text.p: Ghana's ruling party said on Monday one of its supporters was beaten to death in campaign violence ahead of December 7 presidential and parliamentary elections.

The National Democratic Congress (NDC) of President Jerry Rawlings said in a statement the incident took place in the northern town of Kumasi on Sunday. It also reported campaign violence in the capital Accra the same day.

It said an NDC supporter "who was in a convoy of vehicles headig for a rally in Kumasi was brutally attacked and beaten to death by NPP (New Patriotic Party) supporters who also set the NDC office in Kumasi ablaze".

"Irate NPP supporters went on the rampage at Abeka-La Paz in Accra on Sunday, leaving...a number of casualties and a damaged diplomatic car belonging to the British high commission," the statement added.
The NDC called on police to investigate these "barbarous incidents". There was no immediate reaction from the NPP.
A Ghana News Agency report on the Kumasi clash said police called in to restore order fired warning shots from armoured vehicles and used water cannon to disperse PPP supporters.
It said the number of people wounded was not known.
Political parties are wrapping up campaigning for the polls, the second since the restoration of democracy four years ago.
Rawlings, 49, a former military ruler, is seeking a second four-year term as elected leader.
His NDC is challenged by an alliance formed by the NPP and the People's Convention Party, with NPP's John Kufuor as a joint candidate.
Most political analysts predict a close race between the two men although there is also a third candidate -- surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention.
Rawlings, an air force flight lieutenant who took power in 1979, restored civilian rule only to seize power again in 1981.
Kufuor, 57, is a seasoned politician, lawyer and businessman. He has sat in parliament and served briefly as a minister under Rawlings in 1982.
Campaigning has been intense but generally peaceful.

Apart from a well-publicised cabinet brawl between Rawlings and his then vice-president, the last major political flareup in Ghana dates back to May 1995 when five people were shot dead in Accra at an opposition protest against increased value added tax. Witnesses blamed young men wearing T-shirts of the pro-Rawlings Committees for the Defence of the Revolution.
